ECE 6390 / Exam 2

Follow the Connections Back Through the Link

Fig. 138 shows why the chapters belong to one engineering problem: deliver information or infer position using a physical wave. Each arrow changes the question being asked and therefore the quantity, units and assumptions that the next equation needs.

Propagation, interference, and measurement connect the chapters. A travel delay becomes a phase shift; a phase shift changes how fields add; the field sum becomes a power pattern. Normalize that pattern against total radiated power and it becomes directivity. Apply antenna loss and we have gain. Add range and receiving area and we have received power.

On the information side, sampling chooses times, quantization chooses recorded levels, and compression chooses a shorter description. Channel coding supplies protection. Modulation selects a waveform, while pulse shaping and matched filtering help the receiver distinguish the choices at the right moments. Rates tell us how quickly the choices arrive; noise metrics tell us how reliably they can be recognized. Navigation uses a known spreading code to measure timing, Doppler to measure motion along the viewing direction, and several simultaneous pseudoranges to estimate position and the receiver clock together.

The running example carries declared assumptions through the link. Atlanta’s geometry gives 50.8∘50.8^\circ elevation and 37,03137{,}031 km slant range; the assumed 10 GHz frequency gives 203.8203.8 dB free-space loss. The 1 m dish with assumed aperture efficiency 0.600.60 supplies 38.238.2 dBi gain. Together with the independently assumed transmit power and transmit gain, Friis’ equation gives −125.6-125.6 dBW received power. The assumed 290290 K system temperature and 2 Msym/s symbol rate give C/N0≃78.3C/N_0\simeq78.3 dB-Hz and Es/N0≃15.3E_s/N_0\simeq15.3 dB. One 3000-symbol realization then produces zero QPSK and 34 uncoded 16-QAM symbol errors at equal average symbol energy. Those finite counts illustrate decisions before decoding; the rate-one-half code in the rate ledger is a separate bookkeeping assumption, with no decoder or coded error-rate guarantee evaluated. Changing constellation at fixed symbol rate also changes the useful bit rate. Each calculation states its new inputs rather than treating every design choice as a result of the preceding one.

For each link calculation, identify the propagation distance, observation direction, time interval, field or power quantity, and reference level. These definitions connect the equations to the system being modelled.

Practice

1. Double the range while keeping frequency, power, gains and excess losses fixed. How do received power and free-space path loss change?

Use the inverse-square range dependence and 20 log10 of the range ratio.

Received power becomes one quarter, about 6.02 dB lower. Free-space path loss increases by about 6.02 dB. Receiver noise is unchanged if its temperature and equivalent bandwidth are unchanged.
